intro: Royal Leamington Spa is a Regency spa town on the River Leam in Warwickshire, its streets of white stucco laid out when people came to take the waters. One reader has sent us two of its trees, both by the railway viaduct on the west side of town: a wide old oak on a grassy bank at the entrance to Elizabeth Park, and a towering redwood at the entrance to Victoria Park, each with their own measurement of its trunk.
meta_description: Two trees readers found in Royal Leamington Spa: a wide old oak at Elizabeth Park and a towering redwood at Victoria Park, and how to find them.
question_meta: Two trees readers found in Royal Leamington Spa: a wide old oak at Elizabeth Park and a towering redwood at Victoria Park, and how to find them.
question_answer: The Oak at the Gate of Elizabeth Park stands on a grassy bank at the entrance to Elizabeth Park, by Princes Drive in Milverton, and the Redwood at the Gate of Victoria Park stands beside the path at the entrance to Victoria Park, a short walk away. Both are free to visit.
question_context: Both of Royal Leamington Spa's trees on our map came from the same reader, and both stand near the stone arches of the railway viaduct on the west side of town. The first is an oak at the entrance to Elizabeth Park, by Princes Drive: a short, thick trunk that leans a little and breaks into crooked limbs spreading wider than the tree is tall, the open-grown shape of an oak that has never had to compete for light. The reader measured its trunk at 375 centimetres round. The second is a redwood at the entrance to Victoria Park, a red, flared trunk rising far above its neighbours. The reader measured it at 450 centimetres round and calls it a coast redwood; its hanging shoots look to us like a giant sequoia, so we ask readers who know. Those figures are theirs, and we have no planting records for either tree yet. Both parks are public.

faq.q: Where are the old trees in Royal Leamington Spa?
faq.a: An old oak stands at the entrance to Elizabeth Park, by Princes Drive in Milverton, and a tall redwood at the entrance to Victoria Park, a short walk away. Both are near the railway viaduct.
Yes. Both stand at the entrances to public parks and are free to visit.
The reader who sent them measured the oak's trunk at 375 centimetres round and the redwood's at 450. We have no record of their heights or planting yet.

trees.story:
"Magnificent oak tree at entrance to Elizabeth Park," wrote the reader who sent us this tree from Royal Leamington Spa, and the photographs make the case for the word.

It stands alone on a grassy bank by Princes Drive, with the stone arches of the railway viaduct behind it and a new flight of steps running down a white wall beside it. The trunk is short and thick and leans a little, and within a few metres of the ground it breaks into great crooked limbs that spread wider than the tree is tall, the shape an oak takes when nothing has crowded it. In the reader's November pictures the leaves are turning yellow against a clear sky, and the crown reaches out almost to the steps.

The reader measured it: 375 centimetres round the trunk. That is their figure, and a girth like that puts an open-grown oak well into its second century, though we have no record yet of when it was planted or what stood here before the park. If you know, tell us here.

Walk round to the viaduct side to see the trunk against the arches.

trees.story:
"Beautiful Redwood at entrance to Victoria Park," wrote the reader who sent us this tree from Royal Leamington Spa, the same reader who sent us the old oak at the gate of Elizabeth Park a short walk away.

Their two photographs show a tree that dwarfs everything around it. One, taken from the path at its foot, shows a red, flared trunk rising straight past the bare winter limbs of its neighbours, through a narrow dark crown, with the arches of the railway viaduct behind. The other looks straight up the trunk, deeply furrowed and glowing in low sun, into branches hung with long blue-green shoots.

The reader calls it a coast redwood. Those hanging, cord-like shoots look to us more like its cousin the giant sequoia, the Wellingtonia that Victorian towns planted in their new parks, so we ask readers who know to tell us which it is. The reader measured its trunk at 450 centimetres round. That is their figure; we have no record yet of its height or of when it was planted.

Stand at the foot of the trunk and look up, as the reader did.
